claims.text: Loads on a bridge include live loads such as traffic and the dead load of the structure's own weight.

evidence.excerpt: live load - a temporary dynamic load such as vehicular traffic that is applied to a structure
dead load - a static load due to the weight of the structure itself

claims.assumptions: Generic definition of load types; no magnitudes.
claims.intended_visual: LOAD_ARROW on the deck labelled 'Load' (qualitative, not to scale)
claims.scope: conceptual; illustrative models; no member forces, capacities, stresses, safety factors or quantitative comparisons

claims.text: The deck directly supports traffic and is itself supported by the superstructure.

evidence.excerpt: deck - that portion of a bridge which provides direct support for vehicular and pedestrian traffic, supported by a superstructure

claims.scope: conceptual; illustrative models; no member forces, capacities, stresses, safety factors or quantitative comparisons

claims.text: The superstructure is the part of a bridge that provides the horizontal span; it typically includes beams, girders, trusses and the deck.

evidence.excerpt: Structural parts of the bridge that provide the horizontal span.
It typically includes beams, girders, trusses, and the bridge deck.

claims.assumptions: Definition; the cap beams of a timber bent belong to the substructure (pier cap).
claims.scope: conceptual; illustrative models; no member forces, capacities, stresses, safety factors or quantitative comparisons

claims.text: The substructure - abutments at the ends and piers in between - supports the superstructure, and abutments transfer loads from the superstructure to the foundation.

evidence.excerpt: substructure - the abutments and piers built to support the span of a bridge superstructure
abutment - part of bridge substructure at either end of bridge which transfers loads from superstructure to foundation
pier - a substructure unit that supports the spans of a multi-span superstructure at an intermediate location between its abutments

claims.assumptions: Definitions; in the timber model the trestle bents play the role of piers and the banks of the site the role of abutments (illustrative).
claims.intended_visual: CONCEPTUAL_LOAD_PATH from deck through supports to the ground
claims.scope: conceptual; illustrative models; no member forces, capacities, stresses, safety factors or quantitative comparisons

claims.text: A beam spans from one support to another and supports vertical loads.

evidence.excerpt: beam - a linear structural member designed to span from one support to another and support vertical loads

claims.scope: conceptual; illustrative models; no member forces, capacities, stresses, safety factors or quantitative comparisons

claims.text: A beam carries load through its resistance to bending.

evidence.excerpt: As a beam has strength from its bending resistance
girder - a horizontal flexural member that is the main or primary support for a structure

claims.assumptions: Qualitative; no stresses, deflections or capacities. The procedural model has not been analysed.
claims.intended_visual: CALLOUT 'Beams resist bending' on a stringer
claims.scope: conceptual; illustrative models; no member forces, capacities, stresses, safety factors or quantitative comparisons

claims.text: A cap at the top of a bent distributes the loads onto its columns, and columns are vertical members resisting compression.

evidence.excerpt: cap - the topmost portion of a pier or a pile bent serving to distribute the loads upon the columns or piles
bent - a substructure unit made up of two or more column or column-like members connected at their top-most ends by a cap
column - a general term applying to a vertical member resisting compressive stresses

claims.assumptions: Definitions; the posts of the illustrative trestle bents are treated as columns.
claims.intended_visual: CONCEPTUAL_LOAD_PATH stringer -> cap beam -> posts -> ground; REACTION_ARROW at the ground
claims.scope: conceptual; illustrative models; no member forces, capacities, stresses, safety factors or quantitative comparisons

claims.text: A stone arch ring is made of wedge-shaped stones called voussoirs; the keystone is the wedge-like stone at the crown.

evidence.excerpt: Voussoir - one of the truncated wedge-shaped stones composing a ring course in a stone arch
keystone - the symmetrically shaped, wedge-like stone located in a head ring course at the crown of an arch

claims.intended_visual: Frontal exploded close-up of one arch ring; COMPONENT_LABEL 'Voussoirs', 'Keystone'
claims.scope: conceptual; illustrative models; no member forces, capacities, stresses, safety factors or quantitative comparisons

claims.text: The curve of an arch converts vertical loads into horizontal and vertical thrusts at its ends, so the forces within the arch are generally compression.

evidence.locator: Part 2 Ratings, Item 25 Arch, p.144 (manual p.2-56)
evidence.excerpt: The curve converts vertical (gravity) loads within the span to horizontal and vertical thrusts at the spring lines. As a result, the forces within the arch are generally compression
arch - a curved structure element primarily in compression that transfers vertical loads through inclined reactions to its end supports
Arch bridges rely primarily on compression

claims.assumptions: General principle for masonry arches under gravity load; no thrust line, magnitudes or stability assessment of the illustrative model.
claims.intended_visual: CONCEPTUAL_LOAD_PATH along the arch ring from the crown to both springings, styled 'compression'
claims.scope: conceptual; illustrative models; no member forces, capacities, stresses, safety factors or quantitative comparisons

claims.text: An arch transfers vertical loads through inclined reactions to its end supports, and the abutments push inward on the arch.

evidence.excerpt: transfers vertical loads through inclined reactions to its end supports
creating two equal and opposite horizontal forces that push inward on the arch

claims.assumptions: Direction only (inclined, upward and inward on the arch); no magnitudes; the arrow is a support REACTION, distinct from the applied load.
claims.intended_visual: REACTION_ARROW at each springing, pointing up and inward
claims.scope: conceptual; illustrative models; no member forces, capacities, stresses, safety factors or quantitative comparisons

claims.text: A truss is a jointed structure of members arranged in triangles, primarily carrying axial loads.

evidence.excerpt: truss - a jointed structure made up of individual members primarily carrying axial loads arranged and connected in triangular panels
A truss is essentially a triangulated system of (usually) straight interconnected structural elements

claims.scope: conceptual; illustrative models; no member forces, capacities, stresses, safety factors or quantitative comparisons

claims.text: The principal force in each truss member is axial tension or compression.

evidence.excerpt: The principal force in each element in a truss is axial tension or compression.
These axial forces are either compression or tension.

claims.assumptions: Idealisation (pinned joints); the source notes real joints are not perfectly pinned. No member-by-member forces are shown.
claims.scope: conceptual; illustrative models; no member forces, capacities, stresses, safety factors or quantitative comparisons

claims.text: In a simple-span truss under downward loads, the top chord is in compression and the bottom chord is in tension.

evidence.excerpt: The upper, or top, chords are in compression. The bottom, or lower, chords are in tension.
Under gravity loads, the top and bottom chords of the truss provide the compression and tension resistance to overall bending

claims.assumptions: ASSUMPTION: each truss span of the illustrative model is treated as a simple span (separate truss on its own bearings) carrying a downward load. The FHWA source calls this a simplified characterization for the common single-span bridge; continuous spans behave differently. Qualitative only.
claims.intended_visual: CALLOUT on the top chord 'compression (pushed)' and on the bottom chord 'tension (pulled)'
claims.scope: conceptual; illustrative models; no member forces, capacities, stresses, safety factors or quantitative comparisons

claims.text: In a truss, some web members are in compression and others in tension.

evidence.excerpt: Some of these web members will usually be in compression; others will consistently be in tension.

claims.assumptions: General statement; which web member carries which force is NOT shown (no load case analysed).
claims.intended_visual: HIGHLIGHT web members without a tension/compression colour
claims.scope: conceptual; illustrative models; no member forces, capacities, stresses, safety factors or quantitative comparisons
